Can You Turn Off Google Reviews on Your Business Profile?

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

No, a business owner cannot disable Google reviews on a Business Profile: there is no setting for it, and Google treats reviews as public information about a place rather than content the owner controls. Deleting or recreating the listing does not make reviews disappear either, so the workable options are reporting reviews that break Google's policies and managing the rest.

Why there is no switch to turn off reviews

Google's position is that customers have a right to share experiences about a real-world place, and that a profile without reviews would be less useful to people searching on Google Maps. The owner can edit hours, photos, categories and contact details, and can reply to reviews, but cannot decide whether reviews are accepted.

This surprises many Italian business owners, especially professionals such as doctors, lawyers or accountants, who feel that public ratings fit poorly with their work. The profile, however, exists because the business exists at a physical address. Claiming it gives you management rights, not ownership of what the public writes. Every request to turn off Google reviews sent through Business Profile support receives the same answer for this reason.

Restrictions you do not control

Google can temporarily limit new reviews on a profile, for instance when it detects a sudden wave of suspicious reviews linked to a news event, or when a business has been found to solicit fake ones. These measures are applied by Google to protect the system; the owner cannot request them as a feature, and they do not remove reviews already published.

Why deleting the profile backfires

Many owners conclude that if they cannot disable Google reviews, they can at least delete the listing. In practice the decision to delete a Google Business listing almost always makes things worse, because removing your management access is not the same as removing the place from Google Maps.

  • When you remove the profile from your account, the public listing usually stays on Maps as an unmanaged place, with all its reviews still visible.
  • Without an owner, you lose the ability to reply, to correct details and to report reviews through the official channels.
  • Anyone can then suggest edits to your phone number, opening hours or website, including people who want to harm you.
  • Marking the business as permanently closed keeps the reviews online and tells customers you no longer operate, which costs real bookings and calls.

For a restaurant in Rome or a clinic in Milan that still trades at the same address, any of these outcomes is more damaging than the reviews themselves.

The duplicate-profile trap

A second tempting idea is to close the old profile and open a fresh one to start from zero. Google's guidelines prohibit creating more than one profile for the same business at the same location, and its systems compare names, addresses, phone numbers and categories precisely to spot this.

A duplicate is typically merged back into the original listing, bringing the old reviews with it, or suspended altogether. A suspension removes the business from Maps results until it is reinstated, which can take weeks and requires proof of the business's legitimacy. A new profile is legitimate only when something real has changed: a move to a new address, a genuinely new business, or a rebrand following a change of ownership. Even then, Google may decide to keep the reviews attached to the place.

Legitimate ways to deal with unwanted reviews

The effective route is to remove what violates the rules and answer what does not. Google removes reviews that are fake, written by competitors or ex-employees, off-topic, offensive, or that contain personal data, so a careful review of your profile against those policies is the first step.

  1. Flag each problematic review from the Business Profile, choosing the policy that actually applies rather than a generic reason.
  2. Track the outcome in Google's reviews management tool and, where a report is rejected, submit an appeal with a clear explanation.
  3. Collect evidence for reviews that are part of a coordinated attack: dates, patterns, accounts with no history, links to competitors.
  4. For defamatory content, consider the legal route under art. 595 of the Italian Criminal Code or a notice under the Digital Services Act.
  5. Where a review discloses your personal data or health information about a patient, rely on GDPR and, if needed, the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali.

The procedure for each type of report is described in detail in our practical guide to deleting fake and negative Google Maps reviews in Italy.

Reducing the impact of reviews you have to keep

Genuine negative reviews cannot be removed, but their weight on your rating and on customer decisions can be reduced substantially. Two levers matter: how you respond and how many satisfied customers leave feedback.

A calm, factual reply shows prospective customers that the business listens, and it often matters more to them than the original complaint. Avoid arguing, revealing client details or accusing the reviewer without proof; our article on responding to a negative review without making it worse covers the wording in detail. At the same time, a steady flow of recent reviews from real customers pushes older complaints down the list and moves the average. Asking every customer, at the right moment and through a simple link or QR code, is allowed; offering discounts or gifts in exchange for reviews, or asking only happy customers, is not.

You cannot switch reviews off, but you can decide what a new visitor sees first: recent, genuine feedback and professional replies, rather than a single unanswered complaint from years ago.

When removing a listing is the right decision

Removing or closing a profile is appropriate only when it reflects reality. If the business has ceased trading, has moved permanently, or the listing is a genuine duplicate created by mistake, Google offers the right options for each case.

For a closed business, mark the listing as permanently closed and then remove it from your account; the place may stay on Maps as closed, which is accurate. After a move, update the address rather than creating a new profile, unless the old location continues to operate under someone else. Duplicates should be reported through Business Profile support so that Google merges them correctly.
